strengths: Elegant and intuitive core idea: exploiting that the Radon–Nikodym derivative between a diffusion process and its time-reversal is identically one yields a simple identity connecting marginal densities and transition kernels, from which both density estimation (RNDE) and SMC importance weights (RNC) follow naturally.

Strong unifying contribution: the paper rigorously shows that several recent methods that appear distinct — the Itô density estimator (Karczewski et al. 2024; Skreta et al. 2024), the Feynman–Kac density estimator (Huang et al. 2021; Premkumar 2024), the Twisted Diffusion Sampler (Wu et al. 2023), Feynman–Kac Steering, and the Feynman–Kac Corrector (Skreta et al. 2025) — are special cases of RNE/RNC, with detailed proofs (Propositions 2.2, 3.1, C.2–C.5).

Genuine practical value beyond unification: the flexible choice of sampling/target processes (Eqs. 25, 36–38) and the analytic reference process (Section 4) give concrete, plug-and-play design freedom that recovers FKC as a special case and empirically improves performance over FKC/TDS on annealing (ALDP: Energy TVD 0.034 vs 0.338 for FKC) and multi-target SBDD.

Thoughtful treatment of discretisation issues: the analysis in Appendix A.3 (Eq. 45, ∆N ≈ 0.87d for realistic VE schedules) clearly explains why naive Gaussian-kernel estimates are unstable and motivates the reference process; a non-asymptotic O(√∆t) L2 error bound is provided (Proposition A.2).

Broad scope: the framework extends to discrete diffusion (CTMC) with a useful computational argument over Kolmogorov-equation solvers, and the imperfect-model discrete-time weights (Proposition A.1) are exact while the paper honestly discusses when the flexible continuous-time weights may outperform them.

Comprehensive experiments covering density estimation, annealing (ALDP, LJ-13, GMM), product of diffusion models for multi-target SBDD, and reward-tilting, with ablations over (ca, cb) and weight-variance/ESS analysis.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely in unification and generalisation rather than fundamentally new machinery: the key density estimator is theoretically equivalent to the concurrent Itô density estimator (Karczewski et al. 2024; Skreta et al. 2024) — acknowledged in the paper — and the SMC weights recover TDS and FKC as special cases. The incremental technical contribution over these works (free drift hyperparameters, reference process) is real but modest.

Experimental scale is limited: all experiments are on molecules (ALDP, LJ-13, SBDD with 20/15 pocket pairs) or toy Gaussian mixtures; no image, text, or other large-scale pretrained diffusion experiments are presented, leaving the practical reach of the 'plug-and-play' claim on high-dimensional pretrained models unverified.

Density-estimation experiments use an analytically known score (VE process on a 10-D MoG), so behaviour with imperfect learned score networks — the practically relevant regime — is not directly evaluated for RNDE; the paper acknowledges density errors 'can be arbitrary' given imperfect scores.

Gains over FKC depend on task-specific tuning of hyperparameters (ca, cb) and the paper itself states the optimal balance 'can be task-dependent' and that sometimes lower ESS (and collapsed diversity) is preferable; this weakens the plug-and-play narrative and makes some comparisons partially selection-driven. RNC-TDS notably underperforms (e.g., Table 2).

The intermediate target marginals qt (Eq. 18) are heuristically specified, and for reward-tilting the handling of non-differentiable rewards (gt = 0, Tweedie estimate) is ad hoc; no systematic principle for choosing (at, bt) is offered beyond heuristics.

Several rigorous claims are deferred or incomplete: no non-asymptotic guarantee for the reference-free continuous-time RNE ('left for future discussion'), and the authors concede that the q_target = (p_{2:N|1})^β construction 'does not seem to correspond to an SDE in the limit'.

Minor writing issues: typos ('Secections', 'Keynman-Kac', 'controlable'), occasional notational sloppiness (e.g., q0 ∝ (p0^(1) p0^(1))^β in Appendix D.2), and dense derivations that can obscure the main message.

strengths: The paper offers a clean and intuitive unifying perspective: expressing marginal density estimation and SMC importance weighting for diffusion models through the Radon–Nikodym derivative between time-reversal path measures. This is pedagogically valuable and connects several seemingly disparate methods (Ito density estimator, Feynman-Kac density relation, Twisted Diffusion Sampler, Feynman-Kac Corrector, Feynman-Kac steering) under one framework, with formal propositions recovering them as special cases.

The analysis of discretisation-induced instability (Eq. 32, Appendix A.3, Eq. 45/56) is a genuine practical contribution, and the proposed analytic reference process (Section 4) is a sensible fix, accompanied by a non-asymptotic L2 convergence rate of O(√Δt) for the reference-based estimator (Proposition A.2).
The extension to discrete diffusion (CTMC) in Appendix A.5 and the importance-sampling perspective (Proposition 3.1) add breadth and make the framework more generally applicable.

Experiments cover density estimation, annealing (ALDP, LJ-13), multi-target SBDD, and reward-tilting, with ablations over the design hyperparameters (ca, cb) and analysis of weight variance vs. effective sample size.
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty. The central identity (Radon–Nikodym derivative between a diffusion and its time-reversal equals one) is a classical consequence of Anderson/Nelson time-reversal and Girsanov theory, and the authors themselves acknowledge (Section 2.2) that the resulting density estimator is theoretically equivalent to the concurrent Ito density estimator (Karczewski et al., 2024; Skreta et al., 2024). The main new elements are a re-derivation, a unification, and added flexibility in choosing proposal/target processes—an incremental contribution over FKC (Skreta et al., 2025) and TDS (Wu et al., 2023).

The claimed 'plug-and-play' nature is undermined by the need to heuristically tune the hyperparameters (ca, cb) or (λa, λb) of the sampling and target processes. The best configurations are task-dependent (the authors admit this in Section 5 and Appendix B.2), and the headline results in Tables 1–2 appear to come from empirically selected hyperparameter values, raising concerns about selection bias on evaluation metrics.

Evaluation is modest in scale and rigor: density estimation is tested only on a 10-D Mixture-of-Gaussians with exact scores; control experiments are on small molecular systems (ALDP, LJ-13) and SBDD with 20/15 protein targets, 32 ligands each, and very large standard deviations (e.g., 0.345±0.288). There are no experiments on high-dimensional or image-domain tasks, and several comparisons rely on indirect metrics (TVD on histograms) rather than established baselines. The RNC-TDS variant actually underperforms FKC in Table 1.

The theory has acknowledged gaps: the exact weights for imperfect models (Eq. 27, Proposition A.1) 'do not correspond to the RND between two Ito processes' in continuous time (Section 2.3.3), i.e., the exactness claim is only in discrete time under a particular definition of the target, which weakens the theoretical elegance of the framework. The continuous-time instability analysis (Eq. 32) is heuristic rather than a formal bound.

Significance of gains over existing methods is small: when the theoretically equivalent configuration is used, RNC matches but does not clearly exceed FKC; the improvements come primarily from extra hyperparameter freedom whose tuning is not principled. This makes the practical advance over FKC/TDS hard to assess.
No code or reproducibility material is mentioned, despite the reliance on specific discretisation schedules, resampling thresholds, and hyperparameter settings across many components.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and conceptually appealing unification: the observation that the Radon-Nikodym derivative between a diffusion process and its time-reversal is identically one yields a single 'plug-and-play' identity from which density estimation (Itô estimator, Feynman-Kac density relation) and SMC weight computation (TDS, Feynman-Kac steering, Feynman-Kac corrector) can be recovered. The connections are not merely asserted but proven in detail in Appendix C, including explicit derivations recovering FKC for annealing, product, CFG, and reward-tilting cases.

The analysis of instability in the naive discrete-time estimator (Eq. 32, Appendix A.3) is valuable and honest: the paper quantifies the accumulated discretization error of the Gaussian-kernel formulation vs. the continuous-time integral form, and motivates the analytical reference process. The O(√Δt) L2 convergence guarantee for the reference-based estimator (Proposition A.2) is a genuine technical contribution.

The framework offers real design flexibility (free choice of sampling and target drifts a_t, b_t with tunable λ hyperparameters) that strictly generalizes existing methods, and the discussion of the imperfect-model case with exact discrete-time weights (Proposition A.1) and its trade-offs (exactness vs. ESS) is careful and nuanced.

Experiments cover a diverse set of meaningful tasks: density estimation on an analytically tractable GMM benchmark, inference-time annealing on molecular systems (ALDP, LJ-13), multi-target SBDD via model composition, and reward tilting for controllable drug design. The (ca, cb) sweep analysis relating weight variance/ESS to sample quality is informative.
The paper extends the framework to discrete diffusion (CTMCs) with an online likelihood estimator that is cheaper than solving the Kolmogorov equation, and includes a thoughtful limitations section.
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: the core identity (RND of a time-reversal pair equals one) is classical, and the paper itself concedes that the density estimator is theoretically equivalent to the concurrent Itô density estimator (Karczewski et al., 2024; Skreta et al., 2024), the annealing/CFG weights reduce to FKC (Proposition 2.2), and the exact discrete weights recover TDS. The remaining new technical content (flexible drift choices, reference process stabilization, convergence rate) is solid but incremental, and the main framing as a 'unifying perspective' weakens the claim of a fundamentally new method.

Empirical improvements over the closest baseline (FKC) are modest and hyperparameter-dependent. In Table 1, RNC-TDS underperforms FKC, and the best RNC result (ca=0.6, cb=0.4) appears to be the best of a tuned sweep; the paper acknowledges the optimal (ca, cb) balance is task-dependent. There is no principled, automatic procedure for selecting these hyperparameters, which limits the 'plug-and-play' claim in practice.

Scale of evaluation is limited. All experiments are on small/medium-scale problems (up to 10D GMM, 22-atom peptides, 13-particle LJ, small-molecule SBDD). There are no large-scale experiments (e.g., image models, latent diffusion) where stability, accumulated error, and computational overhead of the estimator would be most stressed. Density estimation is never evaluated against likelihood metrics on standard benchmarks (e.g., bits/dim on images) or against more density-estimation baselines beyond the Itô estimator (e.g., Huang et al. 2021, Premkumar 2024 empirically).

Some experimental conclusions lack statistical rigor: result tables have very large standard deviations (e.g., Table 2 'Better than known' 0.589±0.413 vs 0.608±0.390), and improvements over FKC in SBDD are within noise for several columns. The claim of 'visible gain over FKC' is not convincingly supported.

Presentation issues: multiple typos and notation inconsistencies (e.g., 'vaiance-preserving', 'Secections', 'Keynman-Kac', 'often divergence-free', inconsistent use of β in the product definition q0 ∝ (p0^(1)p0^(2))^β vs. (p0^(1))^α(p0^(2))^β, β=2 in experiments vs. α,β formulas), which occasionally make the main results (Table 2, Eq. 23) hard to parse.

The practical benefit of the reference process is demonstrated only in low dimensions; the analysis in Appendix A.3 predicts error growing as O(d), so the stability issue should be more severe in high dimensions, yet no high-dimensional density estimation experiment is provided to validate this directly.

Dependency on heavily concurrent work: since FKC, Itô density estimator, and TDS already exist and are recovered as special cases, the incremental gain of this paper must come from the flexibility/stability results, but the evidence that these translate into consistent practical advantage is not decisive.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely useful unifying perspective: a single identity (RND between time-reversal path measures = 1) that cleanly derives and connects many previously disparate methods (Itô density estimator / density-augmented SDE, Feynman-Kac correctors, twisted diffusion sampler, Feynman-Kac steering, Fokker-Planck regularisation). The connections are not merely asserted but formally proven in the appendix (H.3, H.4, H.5), including a demonstrated strict generalisation ('FKC ⊆ RNC'), which is a real contribution to the diffusion inference literature.

The analysis of the reference-process stabilisation is a concrete and valuable technical contribution beyond the unification: the paper identifies and quantifies the accumulated discretisation error of the naive Gaussian-kernel formulation (Eq. 54, Appendix G.2, with an illustrative Δ_N ≈ 0.87d example) and provides a non-asymptotic O(√Δt) L2 convergence guarantee for the reference-based estimator (Proposition G.1), verified empirically.

Experiments are thoughtful rather than decorative: the (ca, cb) sweep connects weight variance/ESS to sample quality and honestly discusses the diversity-vs-quality trade-off across targets (ALDP, LJ-13, GMM); the multi-target SBDD experiment uses a real pretrained-model pipeline; and the energy-based training results include a quantitative free-energy estimate (Tab. 4) against an MBAR reference, which is a meaningful validation.

The plug-and-play 'macro' implementation (Fig. 7) demonstrates practical usability, and the paper is commendably transparent, including an explicit erratum on a previously incorrect exact-SMC-weight claim for annealing/product and a clear limitations section.

Generality is well argued: the framework applies to stochastic interpolants, bridge models, and CTMCs (Appendix D), with the CTMC extension positioned as a practical speedup over Kolmogorov-equation solvers.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited: the central identity is essentially the definition of time reversal (Anderson 1982) plus Girsanov, and the density estimator is explicitly equivalent to concurrent work (Karczewski et al., 2024; Skreta et al., 2024), while the SMC weights recover TDS/FKC as special cases. The value is in the unification and stabilisation rather than a fundamentally new estimator, which the paper largely acknowledges but which caps its impact as primarily conceptual.

Experimental scope is narrow and confined to small molecular/low-dimensional systems (ALDP, LJ-13, up to 100D GMM, SBDD). Despite claims of generality to other modalities, there are no experiments on CTMC/discrete diffusion, no image or text-scale demonstrations, and the CTMC material is purely theoretical.

The flexible annealing/product variants rely on the 'perfect diffusion model' assumption (Section 2.1.3); under realistic model imperfection the resampled marginals are biased even as M → ∞. This is acknowledged, but the headline generality claim is thus weaker than it appears, and the exact-weight guarantee covers only reward-tilting.

Empirical gains over the closest baseline (FKC) are mixed: the SBDD improvements (Tab. 3) are modest relative to the very large standard deviations, and the optimal (ca, cb) choice is task-dependent (low ESS sometimes helps), leaving hyperparameter selection heuristic with no principled recipe — this partly undercuts the 'plug-and-play' framing.

Some presentation issues reduce polish: minor notational/typographical errors (e.g., 'RND' vs 'RND derivative' in Fig. 1, 'vaiance', 'Keynman-Kac', duplicated 'Computational Resources' lines), the term 'Radon–Nikodym Estimator' is somewhat misleading since the quantity R is an RND, not an estimator of one, and the reliance on an erratum suggests the theoretical claims required careful re-verification.
The inference-time scaling comparison (Fig. 3) is shown for only one system and one (ca, cb) setting, so the claimed better scaling over FKC rests on limited evidence.

strengths: The paper offers a genuinely useful unifying perspective: it shows that many seemingly distinct methods (twisted diffusion sampler, Feynman–Kac corrector/steering, Itô/density-augmented estimators, Fokker–Planck regularisation) are instances of a single Radon–Nikodym identity, which clarifies the field and enables a plug-and-play SMC weight computation.

The framework is technically well-developed: the discrete-time derivation (Definition 2.1, Eq. 10) is accessible and implementable, the continuous-time connection is carefully established, and there are rigorous additions such as an O(√Δt) convergence-rate proof for the reference-based estimator and a quantitative analysis of the discretisation mismatch (Appendix G).
The stability analysis (misaligned kernel variances, analytical reference process) and the ESS/coefficient (c_a, c_b) sweep show real practical insight into when and why the weights misbehave.

The CTMC extension and the application to energy-based diffusion training / free-energy estimation via thermodynamic integration broaden applicability beyond Gaussian diffusion, and the experiments include appropriate baselines (FKC, dual score matching) with reasonable comparisons.
The appendix is thorough, with derivations of the equivalence to FKC variants, proofs of SMC weight correctness, and detailed experimental setups.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core technical contribution: the central identity (RND between time-reversal path measures is 1, connecting marginals and transition kernels via Bayes' rule) is essentially a known/elementary observation, and the paper itself concedes that the density estimator (Eq. 26) coincides with concurrent work (Karczewski et al., 2024; Skreta et al., 2024) and that FKC/TDS are special cases. What remains is a unification-and-flexibility contribution, which is valuable but incremental relative to prior work.

The main empirical application domains are small: annealing on alanine dipeptide and LJ-13, a 100D GMM, and dual-target SBDD with 20 pocket pairs. There are no experiments on the modalities the paper's generalisation claims target (discrete/CTMC experiments are absent despite the framework claiming applicability), and no standard benchmark-scale tasks (e.g., images or large-scale steering), which weakens the significance and generality claims.

The most headline-worthy result — the flexible (c_a, c_b) design space improving over FKC — is heuristic: the gains depend on task-dependent, manually tuned coefficients, and the authors themselves show the optimal setting flips between targets (lower ESS sometimes better). There is no principled guidance for choosing these hyperparameters, and improvements over FKC in Tab. 1/3 are modest and within what could be tuning effects.

Reliability concerns: the manuscript contains an erratum admitting a prior error in the exact anneal/product SMC weights, and the practical variant requires the 'perfect diffusion model' assumption (acknowledged in Appendix B as leading to biased annealing/composition results), while the exact-weight guarantee covers only reward-tilting. This narrows the practical claims.

Known and acknowledged limitations (SMC self-normalisation bias, low sample diversity, resampling burden, weight-variance instability requiring the reference fix) are substantial for the intended inference-time control use case, and the paper does not address them beyond standard SMC practice.

Writing and presentation issues reduce clarity: inconsistent notation and typos ('vaiance', 'Keynman-Kac', 'produce' for 'product', duplicated 'Computational Resources' paragraphs, 'controlable'), and the Kierkegaard framing in the conclusion is stylistic rather than informative. The positioning against Chen et al. (2024) and other RND-based samplers is relegated to an appendix.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is indicated, and several components (heuristic choices of a_t, b_t, reward designs g_t, λ_R, Δt) rely on undocumented tuning that may be fragile to reproduce.

strengths: The RNE identity is a clean and elegant observation that connects marginal densities and transition kernels via the time-reversal property, and the paper does a thorough job of showing how many seemingly distinct methods (twisted diffusion sampler, Feynman-Kac steering/corrector, Ito density estimator, density-augmented SDE, Fokker-Planck regulariser) arise as special cases, with detailed derivations in the appendix.
The framework is genuinely plug-and-play: the SMC weight computation does not require re-derivation per task, and the CTMC extension broadens applicability to discrete diffusion.

The analysis of discretisation instability and the proposed analytical reference process is a valuable practical contribution, supported by both an intuition (Appendix G.1), a quantitative error analysis (Eq. 54/65), and a non-asymptotic convergence rate (Proposition G.1, O(√Δt)).

Experiments cover multiple application domains (inference-time annealing on ALDP and LJ-13, multi-target SBDD ligand design, inference-time scaling, energy-based diffusion training, and solvation free-energy estimation), with reasonable baselines (FKC, Sum score, Dual SM) and useful ablations (sweep over ca, cb; ESS/weight-variance analysis).
The paper is honest about its limitations, including an explicit erratum noting a corrected mistake in previous SMC weight formulations for annealing/product.
weaknesses: The core idea is conceptually simple—essentially Bayes' rule in discrete time and the trivially-1 RND between a process and its time reversal—so the novelty rests primarily on unification and packaging rather than a fundamentally new technique; the density-estimation component is admitted to be equivalent to concurrent works (Karczewski et al., 2024; Skreta et al., 2024).

Experiments are confined to molecular/small-scale targets (ALDP, LJ-13, GMMs, ligand design); there is no evaluation on standard large-scale generative benchmarks (e.g., image data), making the breadth and practical impact of the 'plug-and-play' claim harder to assess.

Gains over FKC are incremental and partly depend on task-specific hyperparameter tuning of (ca, cb); in Tab. 3, differences between FKC and RNC variants are small relative to reported standard deviations, and the theoretical equivalence in the continuous-time limit further blurs the practical distinction.

The flexible design-space contribution relies on a perfect-diffusion-model assumption (exact time-reversal), which is not satisfied in practice; the imperfect-model variant (Prop. 2.2) is restricted to reward-tilting only, limiting real-world applicability for annealing and product tasks.

The paper contains notable typos and writing slips (e.g., 'vaiance-preserving', 'Keynman-Kac', duplicated 'Computational Resources' lines, a formula typo q0 ∝ (p(1)p(1))β in Appendix I.2), which slightly undermines presentation quality for a methods-heavy paper.

The energy-based training application demonstrates improvements over DSM and Dual SM only on small/medium targets (2D/100D GMM, ALDP); the free-energy result (Tab. 4) is a single system with 3 repetitions.
